newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy polls give thumbs down to separatist Bossi.
newsitem.headline: Italy polls give thumbs down to separatist Bossi.

text.p: The Northern League party lost control of Italy's business capital Milan in mayoral elections, dealing a further blow to the firebrand party and its separatist ideals, commentators said on Monday.

Milan's outgoing mayor Marco Formentini, elected in 1993 at the height of the League's popularity, trailed a poor third to opponents from the centre-right Freedom Alliance and the governing centre-left Olive Tree bloc, initial results showed.
"This is the beginning of the end for Bossi," philosopher and centre-right parliamentarian Lucio Colletti said in the newspaper Corriere della Sera.
"The defeat in Milan is a sign the League's thrust is over and that secessionism has put off electors," he added.

With more than one third of the votes counted, Formentini had polled around 19 percent against 41.5 percent for Gabriele Albertini of the Freedom Alliance and 27.2 percent for the Olive Tree candidate, Aldo Fumagalli.
The two leading candidates will face each other in a run-off set for May 11.
The League was completely ignored by voters in the northeastern city of Trieste and failed to make headway in the industrial city of Turin.
"The electors of Turin have opted for Italy, not Padania," commented the League's candidate Domenico Comino, referring to the movement's self-styled "independent" northern region.
Fiery League leader Umberto Bossi brushed off Formentini's defeat and the poor showing in Turin, saying southern Italian "immigrants" in the cities would never vote for his party.
But his right-hand man, Roberto Maroni, disagreed with Bossi's analysis, saying the Milan vote suggested that the middle classes had deserted the League's ranks in favour of the centre-right.
"This is an even worse outcome and it would be good for us to think about it for a bit," he told reporters.

Bossi advised supporters to "go to the mountains" for the second round and not back anyone in the run-offs. "The north has to prepare for the independence struggle to come and not give even half a vote to the parties from Rome," he said.

"We must prepare for the liberation fight which at least in the big cities will not take place in voting booths...this electoral result will accelerate the secessionist thrust," added the outspoken Bossi.
Counting from the elections, for which 9.4 million voters or about one-fifth of the national electorate were eligible, began on Monday morning and official results were due later in the day.
The League rose to popularity at the height of Italy's corruption scandals in the early 1990s through its vociferous attacks on graft, high taxes and central government inefficiency.

But its star has waned since the general election in April 1996, when Bossi's failure to win the balance of power in parliament was followed by a switch from federalism to a separatist agenda and the symbolic declaration of the "republic of Padania".
Recent opinion polls have shown only scant support among north Italians for his cause of full-blooded separatism.
Bossi, renowned for his blunt and colourful language, was fined by a northern Italian court in January for insulting former star anti-graft magistrate Antonio Di Pietro.
He also faces trial this summer for urging supporters at a rally two years ago to hunt down voters of the far-right National Alliance, part of the opposition alliance.
